extracted.intended_audience: women, housewives, and family caregivers (general readers interested in household health and conduct)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive household guidance for women and family caregivers covering stomach/digestive care, general hygiene, nursing the sick, temperance, cheerfulness, and family music. Emphasizes practical routines, manners, and moral duties in domestic life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care of the stomach / digestive organs
rubrics_metrics.description: The digestive organs deserve major consideration; prevention is better than remedial dosing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confine hygiene to remedial measures; soothe rather than punish an irritated stomach. A few hours' fasting followed by slowly eating a little light food (milk-toast or hot beef-tea) is preferred to immediate dosing. Quiet and diet work more wonders than quarts of medicine. Avoid becoming dependent on remedies to ward off indigestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dependence on digestive 'correctives' (soda, pepsin, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many dyspeptics rely on bicarbonate of soda, soda-mint, or pepsin tablets after meals; this creates dangerous dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bicarbonate of soda only occasionally and in small portions; large and frequent doses have been alleged to produce cancerous conditions of the stomach lining. Do not let such remedies become as necessary as habitual snuff or tobacco. If a food disagrees with you, let it alone rather than relying on medicine to counteract it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dietary precautions for sensitive stomachs
rubrics_metrics.description: If your digestive organs are susceptible, be careful about what you eat even when well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid foods that have disagreed with you in the past. Dyspeptics should eschew hot breads, pastry, fried or greasy food, nuts and many sweets. If a pitcher has a tiny flaw it may crack when filled with boiling liquid — similarly a previously sensitive stomach may relapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skin cleanliness and keeping pores open
rubrics_metrics.description: The skin is a principal organ of waste removal and its pores must be kept open to dispose of impurities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use soap and warm water regularly; sponge the entire body daily (especially creases where perspiration accumulates) if you perspire freely. A plunge bath frequently is recommended as it opens the pores and thoroughly cleanses the surface. Do not neglect parts covered by clothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular exercise and moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise should be regular and abundant but not to the point of over-weariness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Housework and walking suffice for most women, though horseback riding, rowing and tennis are beneficial. Do not tax strength to exhaustion. Sleep needs vary; sleep enough at night to avoid daytime drowsiness. Elderly and feeble persons benefit from an occasional nap after midday, especially in warm weather.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventive hygiene over episodic dosing
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for precautionary hygiene and habits rather than occasional 'courses of physic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many people only resort to medicine on principle; cultivate preventive habits (diet, cleanliness, exercise) instead of periodic dosing which can weaken rather than help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to personal health for social good
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual health, especially of girls/women, is a public responsibility because societal institutions and future generations depend on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be reasonably careful about your health not only for your own sake but because the condition of mothers affects future citizens (quotation: 'unless our girls are healthy, the country is not safe').

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheerfulness as a moral and practical duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Cheerfulness is owed to oneself and others; being habitually miserable or indulgent in imaginary woes is condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sentimental self-indulgence and reverence for 'imaginary woe.' Cultivate will-power and habit to keep cheerfulness: work cheerfully, play with whole heart, and practice the 'brave and bright courage' that makes labor light. Balance seriousness and gayety — do not make life a huge joke, but do not prepare for a 'smileless eternity' by banishing all gaiety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of morbid melancholy and sentimentalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentimentalists who revel in grief or 'talk out' pain are contrasted with those who have borne real sorrow; self-indulgent melancholy is seen as folly or selfishness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not cultivate or display imaginary woes for effect. Genuine grief merits sympathy; theatrical or affectation of sorrow is criticized. Habitual melancholy grows like a fungus and should be battled by vigilance and cheerful habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quiet and order in the sick chamber
rubrics_metrics.description: The sick-room must be kept quiet, orderly, and free from disturbance to aid recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforce 'Dr. Quiet' — wear soft slippers, prohibit loud tones and exclamations. Do not whisper (it arouses curiosity); speak in low-pitched undertones. Avoid discussing subjects (especially political/religious topics) that excite the patient. Do not let the patient brood over work or inconvenience they may cause; act rapidly and quietly when tending the room.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleanliness and grooming of the invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: Thorough cleanliness in minutest particulars is essential for a sick person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sponge the patient all over daily when disease permits; cleanse teeth, brush hair, wash face and hands often. Change gowns and sheets frequently; turn mattresses and beat pillows. Air the room often while keeping the patient warmly covered; avoid overheating and chill. Use a flannel 'nightingale' jacket to leave arms free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and portions of food for the sick
rubrics_metrics.description: Food for the sick should be dainty, attractive, and given in small amounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use choicest china and whitest linen; give very little at a time to avoid discouraging appetite. A small, neatly trimmed portion (one oyster, a small chop, etc.) is preferable to a loaded plate. Presentation and pacing of food can stimulate appetite (example: give one oyster at a time and make her think it is a restraint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration of medicines in nursing
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow physician directions precisely and avoid making medicine-giving an ordeal for the patient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not prepare or measure doses in the patient's presence as it may make them nervous; after swallowing, put bottle and spoon out of sight. Carefully follow prescribed quantity and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early home treatment and parental competence (with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Households should know basic early treatments for children's ailments but must be cautious with toxic drugs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a child is feverish, soak feet in hot water, put to bed, and consider anti-febrines like aconite to induce slight perspiration — but aconite is deadly poison and correct dosing is critical (example dose cited: half a drop in a teaspoonful of water every hour for ages 3–6). Mothers are advised to study children's ailments and proper diet; train children to take medicine and follow prescribed diets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual conduct of patient and nurse (self-control and forbearance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both patient and nurse are expected to exercise temper, gratitude, and restraint to make recovery easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patients should not be unreasonably disagreeable or rude; they should try to be gentle and appreciative. Nurses must avoid showing worry or distracted looks, avoid fussing, and display cheerfulness to help morale. Self-control and forbearance on both sides bring sunshine into suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance: abstain from intoxicating beverages that 'make drunk come'
rubrics_metrics.description: The author condemns drinking anything that leads to drunkenness and criticizes social drinking and the glamorization of 'nips' or cocktails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates total abstinence from drinks that can induce drunkenness; social convivialities that encourage weaker companions are condemned. Anecdotes illustrate ruin caused by drinking. The author allows judicious medicinal use of pure brandy, wine and whiskey and small culinary uses (a spoonful in pudding), but warns to omit them if a family member craves stimulants. Suggests severe restriction of liquor sales (only by druggists and by prescription) as an ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not encourage another's drinking; social example matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Helping or tacitly approving a companion's drinking is morally culpable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not put the cup to your neighbor's lips or help hold it there; discretion should guide hosts and family members to avoid contributing to another's descent into inebriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of family music and musical education
rubrics_metrics.description: Family singing and domestic musical education have cultural and social value and were formerly widespread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage singing by note and musical practice at home. Historically, every household used collections adapted for societies and churches; girls were taught the pianoforte. While modern performance may be more expensive and florid, cultivating sight-singing and domestic music-making is presented as desirable.
